speaker: The Chairman
text: Head L, Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE).

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The climate is a two-faced problem, global commons but local impact.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In the latter, Singapore stands out in the world for being prepared to commit public funds today, to ensure the homes and jobs of tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Meanwhile off Pulau Tekong, we have reclaimed a space the size of two Toa Payoh towns for military use.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I must stress that I support our spending on these long-term problems because the time to build and prepare for the future, is now and today.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The problems are real and urgent even as they are long-term and appear distant and far away.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: As human beings, we are all subject to the bias of long-term discounting.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: How can people care about long-term plans if we do not have enough for our daily lives now?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Spending on the National Adaptation Plan can feel disconnected with our needs today.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Put bluntly, many of us simply do not care about these plans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Hence, I would like to ask the Ministry how it intends to engage the public on the need for such adaptation infrastructure?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: How will the National Adaptation Plan build climate literacy and awareness within the community to foster a culture of climate resilience?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Second, we implement these policies based on best current knowledge.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I have also said that the Government has adopted novel solutions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Here, I would like to ask on the progress on Climate Science.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: What partnerships has the Ministry established with international climate research institutions to strengthen Singapore's climate science capabilities?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: How is Singapore enhancing its climate monitoring and forecasting capabilities to better understand local climate impacts and inform adaptation decisions?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Climate change will impact us in many ways.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: If rainfall becomes too heavy, will our current drainage, crest and pump system still suffice to keep out rainwater and floodwater out?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Do we expect building owners to do more to reinforce their infrastructure, like the case of Coastal Protection?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Mr Chairman, I have spoken about the need to spend today for tomorrow and to convince Singaporeans that this is as a matter of national and fiscal responsibility.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I have also asked for a holistic consideration of how science and evidence is brought to our service.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Together, these will help Singaporeans like me, who want to support climate spending, to understand how and why we are doing so, and the careful consideration that goes into spending every dollar, of the billions in public monies committed for the future.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Climate change places going pressure on these interconnected systems.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Whilst Singapore has progressively upgraded drainage infrastructure, it is neither practical nor cost effective to size drains for the most extreme storm events only.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As rainfall intensities are projected to increase, some residual flood risks may need to be managed at community level during extreme events.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Ministry share how Singapore strengthening community flood resilience, including public preparedness and local response capabilities in flood-prone areas?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry consider a map perhaps, or improved alert system?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Ministry provide an update on recent trends in the number of aquacultural farms, including any consolidation or exit and what the trend might indicate about the sustainability of the sector?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These coastal farms are highly sensitive to surrounding marine conditions and have experienced environmental stresses.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Ministry share how aquacultural farms are transitioning towards climate resilience systems, such as hybrid or re-circulating agricultural technologies as well as the take-up rates of support schemes, the extent of transition across the sector and any key challenges in scaling the adoption of such technologies.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond productivity improvements, sustained demand for local produce matters.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To boost local demand amidst import competition, I understand the Ministry work with industry partners to establish an industry level supply and demand aggregator.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Ministry provide an assessment of its effectiveness in strengthening demand for local produce and plans to further support market development?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Climate pressures across our water do not operate in silos.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As risks intensify, adaptation will become more complex and costly.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If our island city state is to be resilient, we must strengthen the integrity of our systems from infrastructure to industry to individuals.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, climate change poses a serious and undeniable challenge for Singapore, carrying profound consequences for both present and future generations.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: As stewards of today's resources, we bear the responsibility of ensuring a sustainable and habitable environment for future Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Even as we take a science-based approach to climate adaptation, informed by climate projections, there will surely be some margin of error and a range of uncertainty for these projections.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Among other factors, they are contingent on the world's carbon emissions.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: A key part to this adaptation is to build our capabilities today to be climate resilient, in order to safeguard our country and our people.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: First, how is Singapore enhancing its climate monitoring and forecasting capabilities so that we can have more accurate projections, as well as anticipate the effects of climate change, such as extreme weather events before they occur?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: How would MSE harness the latest technologies to support our efforts?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Has the Ministry explored leveraging on artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance Singapore's climate resilience initiatives to sharpen our projections?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: I imagine that the work of climate monitoring and forecasting depends on a multitude of factors that can have many permutations and combinations, with potentially extreme consequences if we do not read the forecast right.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: I imagine that the time is ripe for AI to be included in such work and there is much to be harnessed in this regard.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the immediate impacts of climate change are indeed already felt by the public and these have implications on further outcomes, such as health and well-being.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: For example, undertaking prolonged outdoor activities, such as outdoor work or school physical education lessons when there is high heat stress, could increase the risk of heat-related injuries.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: As we enhance our weather forecasting capabilities, how can we better equip the public with timely information to make proactive and informed decisions on their daily activities, in an effort that protect their well-being against the backdrop of extreme weather changes?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, heat resilience is not just an environmental issue.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It is a public health, productivity and infrastructure issue.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: MSE is advancing long-term adaptation through measures such as coastal protection.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But rising temperatures cut across Ministries, sectors and systems.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: We should now move towards a more coordinated framework.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In the battery industry, every additional degree of operating temperature reduces performance and lifespan.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Similarly, higher ambient heat can accelerate infrastructure wear, increase cooling loads and reduce workers' productivity across sectors.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I suggest three areas for a coordinated approach.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: MOM, MSE, MND and the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) should move in step, so that worker safety, urban design and economic productivity are treated as part of the same system.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Second, scale passive cooling as a baseline strategy.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Within one defined zone, we integrate heat stress guidelines, passive cooling design, airflow planning and sensor-based monitoring.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This allows us to quantify the economic impact of adaptation, not just the environmental benefits.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Coastal protection safeguards our long-term national assets and heat resilience will safeguard both our people and our economic systems.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: A coordinated, cross-Ministry approach will ensure we adapt systematically and not in silos.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Chairman, I would like to speak on heat resilience, with a specific focus on vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: While the weather for the past two months has been generally cool and pleasant, we must acknowledge that for the majority of the year and for the foreseeable future, heat will continue to be an issue.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For many Singaporeans, hot weather will continue to be our daily lived reality, but the burden is not evenly shared.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In building a heat resilient Singapore for our vulnerable groups, I have three suggestions.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We already have heat stress advisories and that is a good foundation.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But the guidance can be made more accessible and more targeted.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The question we must ask ourselves is this – who is vulnerable to heat, and do they know about such advisories?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is especially important for children and also the elderly, who may experience health impacts at lower heat thresholds than healthy adults.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In particular, we must also ask ourselves whether these advisories are age-appropriate and are they easy to act on?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, if a child or a senior were to look and to read them, would they be able to say, "Oh, I know when to do what and what I should do?" Accessibility and awareness also depend on language and channels of communication.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We should translate key guidance into major languages and given the target profile that I mentioned, it should not be too wordy or technical.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Such information should be placed in places where it is visible, for example, our schools, community touchpoints, common areas, lift lobbies and hawker centres.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Given that our young, seniors and also migrant workers spend time on social media, we should also disseminate relevant information on such channels.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is especially important because in the period of April to July, because that is where heat is the most intense in Singapore.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Second, allow me to move to household vulnerability.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Heat resilience plans should clearly prioritise those with few coping options.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, one practical way is to prioritise micro-interventions to reduce heat exposure in places that people actually spend time.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, blocks with poor cross-ventilation, blocks where there are few or no air-conditioned areas such as Community Centres, libraries or shopping malls within a short walk and implement micro-interventions.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many outdoor workers cannot choose to avoid peak heat hours.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This could include sector-specific guidelines, more enforcement in construction sites, or practical resources such as having rest areas, hydration access and work-rest protocols that account for real operating conditions.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Chairman, heat and water shapes our national conversation.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Heat shapes how our children play, how seniors exercise and how workers commute.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Water underpins every household, hawker centre, hospital and industry.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These are not abstract matters and these are daily realities affecting comfort, health and economic resilience.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Government has done well through the National Heat Resilience Strategy which manifests in country-wide manuals like the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) Draft Master Plan 2025 to tackle urban heat and mandatory water recycling for water-intensive projects from 2024 to enhance water resiliency.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But more can be done and I will first speak on heat resiliency, then water resiliency.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Children dehydrate faster and regulate body temperature less effectively.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Seniors face risks of heat stress, cardiovascular strain and hospitalisation.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Is the Government focused on cool pavements, reflective materials and putting data-driven heat mapping for vulnerable estates to good use?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: First, extend covered walkways from high-density residential or commuter points to transport nodes, working towards a 100% coverage.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Second, we should provide fundings to ensure all playgrounds and fitness stations, including existing ones, have overhead canopy shelter using heat safe materials such as tensile fabric membranes.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Outdoor play for children and active ageing for seniors can then be an achievable national reality.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If heat is our daily pressure, water is our strategic safeguard and I have a soft spot for any topic related to water, having begun my first full-time job as an industrial wastewater plant engineer and witnessing the opening of the first large-scale NEWater plant in Changi East more than 16 years ago.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: My career journey reminds me how innovative we have been as a nation with our water strategy despite limited land and no natural aquifers.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Much has been said about the Four National Taps, but may I ask the Ministry to update this House on our latest water strategy, considering climate change?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: What proportion of water comes from each source today, compared with 10 years ago?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Also, we often discuss how we obtain water, but less about how much we lose.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I have received reports from the Management Corporations Strata Title (MCSTs) I care for about burst pipes, suspected to be linked to nearby national construction projects.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: What safeguards has the Ministry done to prevent infrastructure damage and reduce non-revenue water loss?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Water resiliency is not only about diversifying supply.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is also about protecting every drop that we produce.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: By planning ahead for cooler neighbourhoods and secure water systems, we protect our children, seniors and our future.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: So, let us continue that tradition with clarity and with resolve.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: As we launched the Beverage Container Return Scheme this year, we have a critical opportunity to harmonise and strengthen our entire recycling infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: While construction and demolition waste achieved 99% recycling rates, household recycling rates tells a different story.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Much of what enters our blue bins is incinerated or exported rather than truly recycled.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: First, leverage Government procurement power to create guarantee demand for recycled materials.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Expanding our existing green procurement frameworks to mandate minimum recycled content in construction materials, packaging and office supplies would provide the certainty recycling operators need for investment.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This market signal would ripple across the private sector.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Third, upgrade our blue bin system progressively through pilots in new estates.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Introducing organic waste segregation first supported by smart bins with contamination sensors.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Singapore's zero waste ambition requires recycling that actually recycles.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Our citizens deserve a system with environmental integrity and economic viability.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: After years of public education on the importance of recycling, more Singaporean families now make it a point to decontaminate and sort their recyclables before depositing them at the blue recycling bins located near their HDB blocks.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, some practical problems persist for housing estates where the smaller 660-litre recycling bins on wheels are deployed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Appointed waste collectors already undertake collections three times a week.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is partly driven by the growth of online shopping and the increased disposal of packaging material from online purchases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When bins overflow and recyclables are left exposed for longer, the prospects for recyclable contamination increases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What were perfectly recyclable items in and around the bin at the point of disposal, can be rendered unrecyclable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As an ecosystem, such developments can undermine the very recycling behaviour we have worked hard to cultivate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While I understand that NEA can mandate additional collections on an ad hoc basis, does the Ministry not agree that more frequent collection must keep pace with improved and more widespread recycling habits among residents?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chair, over the past months, my residents and fellow Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) Members of Parliament (MPs) have taught me that sustainability is not just a policy goal: it is a way of life.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: From our Nee Soon Green Fest to our zero-waste initiatives, we see what is possible when people take ownership.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Nationally, the upcoming National Adaptation Plan will push this agenda even further.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: But feedback from the ground is clear: we can and must do better.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: With Semakau Island filling up, every avoidable bag of waste is not just trash.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: It is a countdown to the day we run out of space.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Second, what are the public consultation plans for the National Adaptation Plan and what measurable indicators will assess impact at the community level?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Third, we celebrate businesses that cut emissions for quick wins, but too often, adaptation, the very investments that would shield us from floods, heatwaves and other climate shocks, is ignored.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Because the returns are long-term, less visible and harder to measure.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: How will the private sector be incentivised to invest meaningfully in the adaptation measures?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: If we do not rebalance mitigation and adaptation, we risk building a future that looks good on paper but falters under real climate stress.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Singapore's overall recycling rate remains above 50%, but this figure is stabilised by industrial waste streams that are almost fully recycled.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is estimated that the manufacturing of plastics consumes the same amount of fossil fuel as the entire aviation industry, and at the same time used plastics.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Used plastics can hold a high economic value if recycled.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Why manufacture new plastics and increase our carbon footprint when we can reuse recycled ones?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With the climate warming and Semakau expected to be full by 2035, our margin for error is narrow.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This gap between headline performance and material outcomes points to a deeper structural issue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They concluded that plastics recycling rates will not change unless the demand for recycled plastic increases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At the same time, Singapore's recycling system is highly exposed to global market conditions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When demand for recycled materials weakens, when freight costs rise, or when importing countries tighten contamination rules, exporting recyclables become expensive or unavailable.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This was most evident following China's national salt policy and similar measures elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In such conditions, market actors respond rationally by choosing the cheapest available option, which is often incineration.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Incineration reduces landfill volume, but plastics are fossil fuel-based and their combustion releases fossil carbon into the atmosphere.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Because these emissions are accounted for as waste disposal, rather than climate impact, poor plastics recovery can be offset rhetorically by energy recovery.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The material outcome, however, is the destruction of recyclable plastics and a continued reliance on new manufactured plastics.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This creates a risk that incineration is presented as environmental performance when the outcome is that more fossil fuel may be consumed while sustaining a reality where incentives to improve recycling remain weak.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If we truly want to transit to a circular economy as laid out by the Singapore Green Plan, it is imperative that we build an ecosystem that sustains recycling even when external market conditions deteriorate.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This would shift costs upstream, improve packaging design and fund the collection and sorting capacity needed for meaningful recycling.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such a practice has been mandated by the European Union, as well as the state of California.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Government can also use public procurement as a market anchor.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, Switzerland's Swiss Plastic Pipe Recycling Initiative is working to establish a take-back and recycling system for plastic pipes used in civil engineering and building construction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There is strong potential for recycled plastics to become a strategic material —

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Chairman, as we navigate the challenges of climate change, it is imperative that we, as a community, take collective action to build a more resilient and eco-conscious Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our efforts today are directed towards securing a livable environment for our future generations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Before Budget 2026, as part of our regular People's Action Party (PAP) Climate Action Group outreach engagements, my GPC Parliamentary colleagues, Ms Poh Li San, Mr David Hoe and I jointly organised an event based on the theme "Sustainability Living: Creating Zero Waste and a Circular Economy".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It was a robust discussion session with over 30 climate activists, community leaders and stakeholders who came together to discover existing measures as well as new ways for us to foster sustainability in our daily lives.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From the lively discussions and brainstorming, what we have gleaned is this: to convince Singaporeans to adopt green habits that minimise generation of waste, energy consumption, and water usage, three key pillars must undergird our efforts and policies.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One, increasing education; two, improving infrastructure; and three, enhancing incentives.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While sustainability is a global mission, the Singapore way has to be one that is “Made to Measure” and “Measure to Manage," for our unique urban context, with clear metrics to track progress and refine our approaches as we continue on this unceasing sustainability journey.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We need targeted and a range of policies that would in aggregate resonate with and manage everyday Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Against this backdrop, I raise several questions for MSE’s response today.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: First, on the effectiveness of the Disposable Carrier Bag Charge.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This nudge has encouraged many to bring reusable bags, cutting down on plastic waste that clog our landfills and oceans.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, as we approach the three-year anniversary of the Disposable Carrier Bag Charge, I would like to ask the Ministry: what is the latest data on the scheme's overall effectiveness in reducing disposable bag consumption across Singapore?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What lessons can we apply to broader waste reduction efforts?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is heartening to see such incentives making sustainable choices more accessible.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Drawing inspiration from innovative local programmes like the Northwest Community Development Council’s (CDC's) Green Homes at Northwest, which rewards residents with up to $500 in e-vouchers for adopting eco-friendly practices such as using climate vouchers for high-efficiency appliances, I propose MSE considers how we can build on this momentum.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can the Ministry share whether the climate vouchers scheme will continue beyond 2027, or if a nationwide version akin to Green Homes at Northwest, perhaps with tiered rewards for multiple green actions, could be rolled out to amplify incentivisation and education across all districts in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By making producers responsible and consumers active participants, it addresses waste at its source while improving recycling infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To ensure its success, can the Ministry provide more details on how the scheme will be operationalised, including management of unredeemed deposits and strategies to garner widespread support from Singaporeans through education campaigns and accessible return points?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The BCRS may only be as successful with the public’s support.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, as we have heard the views of affected proprietors and feedback from consumers, the greatest challenge that needs to be overcome is in my opinion getting everybody on board.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This milestone is a testament to ground-up action.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In closing, embracing a green sustainable lifestyle is not just about policies – it is about empowering every Singaporean to make a difference.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By prioritising education, bolstering infrastructure and enhancing incentives, we can measure our progress and manage our resources wisely.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Mr Chairman, thank you for allowing me to speak on this important topic.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: It is no great stretch of reasoning to surmise that this is because the original goal is thought to be out of reach – to fail to reach a target, by itself, is not a great failure.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: In policy making, as it is in sports, and in life, stretched targets are important.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: At the same time, there are two important differences.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: First, benchmarking. "30% of our food needs by 2030" cannot have been a target based on a simple gimmick of two numbers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: It must have been made based on some policy assumptions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Can the Minister tell us what among its initial assumptions failed?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: These include – first, what lessons are learnt from the failures of businesses in big-scale urban farms and plant proteins?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What can MSE do differently now to step up local produce?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Second, the new food targets are different compared to the past in that they are more targeted to specific food types.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Can the Minister explain how these targets have emerged.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: For example, are they due to the specifics of Singapore’s land size and our comparative advantages?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Again, targets must be set based on specific and objective assumptions, and it would be useful to hear from the Minister what these are.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Last, even as we strive towards these new targets, we must remember that most of our food remains imports.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Can I ask the Minister about our food source diversification and global partnerships?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: While those with deep pockets will continue to enjoy a wide variety of fresh foods, the average Singaporean may have to restrict themselves and change their diets.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: We do not need to ensure that everyone has asparagus and truffles, but we do want to make sure that fresh fish and vegetables are not out of reach for most homes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: When I say “produce”, I mean we waste the food that we have bought, cooked and flown halfway across the world on very expensive trade routes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Even as MSE works out a strategy to procure more food, we must at the same time, waste less.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Can the Minister tell us of plans and efforts to reduce food waste?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, I would like to speak on three of the four pillars of our Singapore Food Story 2, diversifying imports, global partnerships and growing local.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I would also like to declare my interest as someone on a plant-based diet.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: First, I would like to seek clarification on how diversifying our imports and global partnerships differ in practice.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Diversification spreads sourcing risk across multiple countries and suppliers.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Global partnerships appear to go deeper, involving structured agreements, upstream cooperation and mechanisms that can be activated during disruptions.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This reminds me of my days as a junior officer in Enterprise Singapore working on the Singapore-Sino Jilin Food Zone.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: However, replicating similar structured flows across other food categories proved more complex.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: First, how do we assess whether a global partnership extends beyond a single category of products?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: If a partnership secures supply for one staple commodity, does it meaningfully support diversification efforts across other food types such as protein, fresh produce or processed foods?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Second, what threshold qualifies an arrangement as a “global partnership”?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Clarifying this will help us understand whether our partnerships are commodity-specific arrangements, or broader strategic platforms that can support food resilience across multiple segments.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: On growing local, we have focused largely on eggs and fish.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But I would also encourage us to continue strengthening our position in plant-based and alternative proteins.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Global investment in this sector has slowed and adoption has been uneven.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: However, from a food resilience perspective, plant-based and alternative proteins remain strategically relevant.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This allows us to move from grow local to produce local even within our land constraints.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Food resilience is not only about having enough food in terms of quantity.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It is also about nutritional stability, particularly the reliability of our protein supply.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: If we clarify how diversification and global partnerships work together, and continue to invest in future protein capability, we can strengthen both immediate supply resilience and long-term strategic depth.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: However, while the timeline has shifted, the urgency has not.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: We face a global environment where supply chains are increasingly vulnerable to disruption.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: In this context, strengthening our local food capabilities is not just an economic ambition – it is a strategic necessity for our survival.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: First, beyond the feasibility study on the new multi-tenant facility, how will the Ministry further support our existing local food producers to succeed even in spite of high costs?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Are there plans to help them access better financing or technology to ensure both survival and ability to scale?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Second, I understand 11 agencies are currently required to approve a plan for commercial farming.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Will the Minister also consider allocating resources towards engagement of food producers to provide them with support to meet regulatory guidelines and requirements?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Will there be a review to identify if it would be possible to streamline regulatory processes?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Third, achieving our food security goals requires an "all-hands-on-deck" approach.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: By setting aside more community spaces into community plots and growing public interest in community farming, we can not only supplement our food supply but also strengthen our "we first" Singapore spirit, engaging our citizens directly in stewardship of our food security.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Before 1940s, Teochew-run kelongs accounted for nearly half of almost 400 sea farms.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a Teochew-nang and all of us as residents of Pulau Ujong, or what some call Mainland Singapore, the nautical way of life is close to our nation’s heart.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Recently, I visited open cage fish farmers offshore with fellow PAP MP Valerie Lee.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Farmers shared that while they can meet production targets, they struggle to compete with cheaper imports.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To ensure our farms thrive and as follow up to Parliamentary Questions I have filed, I have three suggestions.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The first, in supporting public accessibility, I note that visits to sea-farms are "not encouraged" due to biosecurity concerns.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the Government provide technical and financial support to help farms meet these standards?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Managed public access is a vital tool for education and brand-building.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Without this data, we cannot address the long-term manpower resilience of the sector.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, will the Ministry partner with Singapore Tourism Board and National Heritage Board to integrate sea farms into heritage and tourism products?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Telling the story behind our food can drive local demand necessary for food security.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, if sea-based farming is a pillar of our resilience, we must protect its viability.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In 10 years, will open-cage fish farming remain part of our food story or merely our history?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, I declare my interest working in the supply chain sector.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I believe for these strategies to be to be successful, we will need to forge a strong alliance between our food and supply chain logistics sectors.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, we have to go beyond diversified imports to diversified imports with integrated logistics.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our efforts to diversify our food sources will only be as successful as our ability to transport them safely to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For many products, a new source is useless if the cold chain breaks.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, I suggest that the Government support the set-up of shared digital platforms where importers and logistics providers are able to track "source contamination risks", work out alternative sources and transport pathways to Singapore, in real-time.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, going beyond growing local to growing local costs effectively through shared infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To make our high-tech farms commercially viable, we will need shared plug-and-play logistics hubs that consolidate cold storage and first-mile, last-mile distribution.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will help to bring down distribution cost for producers and make our local produce much more cost competitive.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our strategic stockpiling of rice and proteins relies on the ability of the supply chain partners because they are the guardians of the reserves.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should encourage our food producers, retailers and supply chain partners to work together, to develop innovative technologies and strategies that enable our food to last longer, while also generating less waste.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And finally, going beyond developing global partnerships to transforming Singapore into the regional distribution centre for high-value food.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should leverage our world class port-infrastructure and invite food firms to use Singapore as their re-export base, where products are processed, certified by SFA standards and redistributed across the region.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will give us strategic leverage and early-access visibility to global food flows that others lack.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chair, as we develop Our Food Story 2, I believe it is time to build our hawker story too.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government also invests significantly to build and upgrade hawker centres, without recovering the costs from Socially-conscious Enterprise Hawker Centres (SEHC) operators or stall owners.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is part of the social compact between the Government and our people, and our hawker centres and culture have become a central part of our national identity.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I would like to raise two points that I believe will influence our hawker culture in the decade to come.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, while our Pioneer hawkers still make up 30% of cooked food stallholders, this proportion will drop sharply over the next decade as they age.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of them are already operating their stalls with the help of their family members, relatives or stall assistants.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If it is the latter, then it must follow that the average or mean rent of our hawker stalls will go up over the next decade, because 30% of stalls is a substantive proportion, and the jump from $300 to $1,250 is more than a four-fold increase.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their children, who are now also in their 50s to 60s, have come to me.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They want to take over the stalls from their parents but are worried of the rental spike when they do so.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand that it is not realistic or practical to expect the rents of these stalls to be retained at $300 in perpetuity.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I would like to seek MSE's consideration to stretch out the rental increase over a much longer period.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since 2025, NEA has allowed hawkers to hire Long-Term Visit Pass (LTVP) and LTVP+ holders.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chair, I appreciate the expansion of the pool of stall assistants.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, my view is that as long as the head of the stall is a Singaporean, physically present daily at the stall and producing familiar hawker food, it does not matter as much the nationality of his or her stall assistant.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, to further support our long-serving hawkers manage their manpower needs and costs, I urge MSE to re-consider allowing work permit holders to work as stall assistants in our hawker centres, for stalls that have been operating for more than 10 years.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Ultimately, the familiarity that all Singaporeans seek most in our hawker centres is the food, not the stall assistant.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I believe this is a step in the right direction, amidst rising operational costs and long working hours, providing budget meals, eat away at the already thin profit margins of our hawkers, who often have to compromise budget meals' nutritional value to compensate for their diminished profit margins.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Nonetheless, stallholders in SEHCs continue to offer such value meals as centre operators are required to ensure the availability of affordable meal options.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It was also revealed last year that stallholders at Bukit Canberra were contractually bound to provide free meals for low-income residents at their expense, although this was subsequently scrapped.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Although many Singaporeans feel the pinch of rising hawker food prices, it is unfair for our hawkers to shoulder the direct responsibility for providing affordable meals.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have shared in my speech on the Hawker Motion in 2024, the Government could provide discounts for lower-income Singaporeans based on their CHAS card type.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As it is, cardholders who present their CHAS card at the participating eatery would be able to receive a discount on their food, the quantum of which corresponds to the colour of their CHAS card, whether it is blue, orange or green.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Rather than subsidise high net worth individuals who, like low-income households, all receive the same CDC vouchers, the subsidy will be better directed to those who need it the most.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With this, the responsibility of ensuring the affordability of well-balanced and nutritional meals will be shared in a much more equitable fashion across stakeholders, a point which I have shared in a Parliamentary Question in 2025.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: By enhancing governmental support to ensure affordable meals, while securing the livelihoods of our hawkers, younger players could come in and rejuvenate the hawker scene, while sparking the trend of a rising number of veteran hawkers calling it quits and retire.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Chairman, I would like to speak on a very practical aspect of a liveable environment and that is pest control, and this is a case for MSE and NEA to play a stronger role as a national aggregator.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Many residents experience pest issues daily and lead to frustration, including things rodents and cockroaches, and if left unchecked, these problems can become a public health.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: I am sure many of you here have received feedback from our residents in this regard.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: So, I want to suggest that MSE and NEA can do more as a national aggregator for pest control so that we can build a more liveable environment.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: To be clear, I am not advocating for the agencies to take over the municipal responsibilities from Town Councils.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: But what it means is using the strengths as the national agency to raise baseline standards.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: First, MSE and NEA can set clearer common service standards.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: These would address questions, for example, what should the expected response time be when there is a high-risk hotspot, what constitute an adequate follow-up; and also, what is an acceptable recurrence rate?

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: If we define these standards clearly, it becomes easier for all of us to hold vendors accountable and to assure residents that you get the same basic level of service applied regardless of constituency.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Second, there is a case to pool demand and provide shared capabilities because some Town Councils might not have the ability or scale to be able to maintain specialised teams or a surged capacity when a sudden outbreak happens.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: So, a national aggregator can allow for specialised teams, better diagnostics and faster mobilisation when multiple estates are affected.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Third, this can be operationalised through a whole-of-Government demand aggregation contracts with standard key performance indicators and outcomes.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: If we measure these outcomes consistently, we can compare performance, learn what works and raise standards across all board.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: A case in point to why a demand aggregation might be useful is a case of catching chickens.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: So, by having a demand aggregation, we can reduce cost variance and achieve similar outcomes.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Advisories for food operators and residents in relation to pest control should remain current, multilingual and practical.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Education and enforcement on waste management, food handling practices and environmental cleanliness. should be targeted and sustained.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: This topic has been brought up in this House multiple times.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: But we must continue to place attention on this silent killer.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: To be clear, it is not to police what happens inside homes, but to stop smoke from drifting into neighbours' units and harming our young and old.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: There is a need for stronger enforcement powers and smarter surveillance.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: How effective are current measures in addressing complaints on second-hand smoke and also high-rise littering?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Catching offenders in the act is difficult and existing cameras are limited by angles and privacy constraints within homes.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: As a result, recalcitrant offenders act with a sense of immunity, and many complaints reach a dead end for lack of evidence.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: MSE is already using AI video analytics for rat surveillance and drainage inspections.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: It is time we apply this strategic advantage to protect our residents' health, safety and living environment.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: With this, we can overcome the privacy hurdle that currently prevents enforcement.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: Did you know Singapore has 8,000 kilometres of ABC waterways, 17 reservoirs and yet, only 15 designated fishing spots?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: We lament that our children are addicted to screens and thus must do more.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: To encourage them to spend time outdoors, children and youths I have met in Toa Payoh turn to fishing to manage stress and connect with nature.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: However, with no designated fishing spots in close proximity, they resort to fishing in unauthorised and often more dangerous areas, areas with high human traffic, fast water currents or precarious physical barriers.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: Often, youths fishing illegally are met with negative public sentiment or disproportioned aggression.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: If we want our youths to be the stewards of our environment and their outdoor safety, we must first allow access to legal and safe interactions.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou
text: I ask the Ministry to consider opening more designated fishing spots within our reservoirs and waterways by providing convenient and legal access, move away from culture — Thank you.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Chairman, with 30% of Singapore barely above sea level, climate change threatens our home.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Beyond enhancing our infrastructure, we must recognise the vital role of civic society and youth in climate resiliency.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Groups like SeaKeepers Society Singapore lead youths-driven marine initiatives from biodiversity conservations and ocean clean-ups to reducing plastic and engaging communities in science.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Their work strengthens coastal defence, builds regional stewardship and raises public awareness.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I urge structured support through co-funding, grants and mentorship so young advocates can actively contribute to national planning.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Coastal protection is more than engineering; it is a whole of nation effort.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Let us empower our youths, together safeguard our seas and our future.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In Mandarin):   Let us empower our youths, and together safeguard our seas and our future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Chairman, my family welcomed a new member, my granddaughter Ning, this year with great delight.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Her arrival has made me think differently about the future – her future and the future of the world she will live in.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I now want to be fit enough to play with her.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I hope to live to see her graduate from college, and she brings new meaning to my work in the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Numbers like net-zero at 2050, mean sea level rise by up to 1.15 metres in 2100, no longer seem so abstract.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: What kind of world will she live in?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Will she enjoy bliss and stability, or will she confront chaos, losses and disasters regularly in the prime years of her life?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: You see, we are confronting two powerful and interconnected challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Records are being broken in recent years – the hottest year, most intense rainfall, heaviest snowstorm, longest wildfires.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Disruptions in food production and water supply may become frequent occurrences.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Economic instability and geopolitical contestation, like the latest conflict in the Middle East, are clouding our focus on protecting our environment.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Major emitters may backslide on their climate obligations as they grapple with the global tensions on security, energy, trade and investments.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In such uncertain times, the environment becomes an inevitable casualty, and our planet will face the impacts of climate change more severely and sooner.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Singapore will not be spared from these impacts.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our water and food security will be threatened by more frequent supply disruptions and shortages.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our businesses will likewise face climate risks such as damaged infrastructure, reduced productivity and supply chain disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Businesses that have invested in other parts of the world will face similar risks.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Intensifying heat not only makes daily life uncomfortable, but affects our health, safety and even our way of life.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is not a pretty world to bring Ning into.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But as Prime Minister Wong said, we are not mere passive bystanders.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In an increasingly volatile world, we must prioritise building a climate-ready Singapore now.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We must prepare our infrastructure, businesses and people today to be resilient in a climate-impaired future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As Ms Poh Li San and Ms Nadia Samdin have pointed out, strengthening our resilience requires collective action of all segments of society.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Government will lead in our national climate adaptation by identifying climate risks and developing long-term adaptation strategies.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Where necessary, we will invest in infrastructure protection.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Through GreenGov.SG, we will spearhead adaptation efforts and encourage the private sector to follow.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The private sector will include climate adaptation as part of their core business strategy.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: By conducting climate risk assessments, protecting workers, investing in infrastructure, diversifying supply chains and insuring against climate hazards, companies can protect themselves from larger losses and reassure their investors.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Businesses must be able to ride through extreme whether events and resume operations as quickly as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Those who innovate and adapt will thrive in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: All segments of the community will build climate resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Schools can adapt their students' attire and activities and their classrooms to the heat.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Sports organisations can adjust training schedules and enhance their facilities for safety during extreme weather.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Grassroots groups can organise emergency preparedness drills for heatwaves, haze, or floods to strengthen community resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Each of us can build resilience in ourselves and in our family – look out for our neighbours in times of haze, manage our household's food and water supply with contingency and familiarise ourselves with emergency response plans.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It involves a comprehensive review of our adaptation measures across key domains such as heat resilience, coastal and flood resilience, and water and food resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will strengthen and coordinate heat resilience efforts across the whole-of-Government.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will invest more in research and development (R&D) to deepen our understanding of heat impacts, develop innovative cooling solutions and identify effective behavioural changes.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Senior Minister of State Janil will share more details.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Ms Poh asked whether our drainage infrastructure will still be sufficient if rainfall gets heavier in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We regularly review the adequacy of our drainage infrastructure, taking into account the latest drainage design standards and climate projections.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Besides drainage improvements, building shared responsibility and fostering community resilience will remain key flood resilience strategies.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary will share more later.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The studies recommended replacing tidal gates and raising the dykes that are protecting our western reservoirs – a significant source of our water supply.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Site-specific studies for Sentosa and the Southwest Coast will commence this year.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As we reshape our coastlines for the future, we will work hand-in-hand with stakeholders to co-create solutions that not only protect our shores and preserve the spaces and features we value most but provide opportunities to create new spaces.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will continue to innovate and take collective action to ensure Singapore's basic needs are met even in times of disruption.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Senior Minister of State Zaqy and Senioe Minister of State Janil will elaborate.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have touched on the "why" and "what" of adaptation.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A holistic adaptation plan needs to be grounded in and guided by science.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Members asked how we are enhancing climate monitoring and forecasting capabilities, including through international partnerships.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Last September, we established the Climate and Weather Research Alliance Singapore (CAWRAS) to advance tropical climate and weather research for Singapore and Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Of the programme's projects, one covers the use of AI to enhance predictions of heavy rainfall and strong winds, improving our ability to forecast weather phenomena like Sumatra squalls.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Another will develop a high-resolution historical weather record, allowing Singapore and Southeast Asia to identify trends and provide insights into regional climate dynamics.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These efforts position Singapore as a regional leader in climate and weather science through AI-powered forecasting capabilities that enable evidence-based policy-making.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have forged partnerships with leading climate and weather science institutes.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NEA is a core partner in the multilateral Momentum Partnership, a consortium of major operational weather centres and climate research centres.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NEA also has bilateral agreements with major research organisations in Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will augment our climate and weather monitoring capabilities and give the public more accurate heat stress alerts through the myENV app, enabling everyone to protect ourselves from heat.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Together, these advancements will help us make more timely and better decisions from early warning of climate hazards, our food diversification strategy to our long-term adaptation plan.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As climate change affects everyone, it is important for all Singaporeans to have the opportunity to shape our National Adaptation Plan.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Ms Poh and Ms Lee Hui Ying asked how we plan to engage communities on this.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This year, the Government will conduct a series of engagements, including focus group discussions and a public exhibition.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will discuss why climate adaptation is important to all of us and why we need to prepare now.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We hope people can share their experiences dealing with the impacts of climate change, and their ideas on how they can also play a part in Singapore's adaptation efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: By tapping on the collective minds of citizens, businesses and civil society, we will enhance our nation's climate resilience to safeguard our way of life, including those with more needs – the elderly, the young and the low-income households.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For businesses, we will engage and partner our industries in developing adaptation strategies that are tailored to their business needs.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will provide more details later this year and welcome Singaporeans' active participation.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Government is fully aware that there are many community stakeholders who are passionate about climate action and have innovative ideas on adaptation.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To encourage ground-up initiatives, the SG Eco Fund will broaden its funding scope to include adaptation.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Anak, a local design agency, realised that there is a huge gap in how we dress for the heat.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: So, they brought together artists from around the world for a showcase on climate-adaptive fashion.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They ran workshops, raising awareness about urban heat challenges and teaching participants how to create their own heat-mitigating accessories, turning awareness into action and inspiring new ways of living in a warming world.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I am wearing one of their pieces today, the Ultra Sarong.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This scarf, adapted from the Sarong, changes colour from yellow to orange when exposed to the sun, giving you a visual alert to UV exposure.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We welcome more of such brilliant ideas from the community.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary will share more about how the Government will support.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: No single Ministry, agency or sector can do this alone.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Businesses must innovate, communities must support one another and researchers must push boundaries.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Whether in exploring ways to better manage heat, how to be prepared for flash floods or how we can implement measures while preserving recreational spaces and biodiversity at our coastlines, public participation will determine the effectiveness of our long-term plans.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Chairman, as a new grandmother, I hope that my granddaughter can grow up in a peaceful and stable environment.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: However, even though our country does its utmost to protect the environment, environmental changes occurring elsewhere will still affect us.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In this world full of uncertainties, I hope that my granddaughter can grow up with resilience and confidence to meet the challenges ahead of her.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Chairman, we are experiencing the effects of climate change today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This requires a multi-pronged approach, which includes enhancing water resilience, heat resilience and resource resilience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: At the heart of all our adaptation efforts is the importance of collective action.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Government agencies, businesses, community groups and individuals, all of us have a part to play.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Valerie Lee asked about our water resilience efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are a small island nation with limited natural water resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Through strong national determination, long-term planning and innovation, we have built a robust and diversified supply of water over decades with our four national taps: local catchment water, imported water, NEWater and desalinated water.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: A recent UN report has declared that the planet has entered global water bankruptcy, with long-term water withdrawals exceeding renewable inflows in many regions across the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is crucial that Singapore continues to plan ahead and invest in water infrastructure, so that our water needs continue to be met.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Construction of DTSS 2 has progressed well, with the deep tunnels substantially completed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: PUB is also carrying out a feasibility study of a potential sixth desalination plant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: With climate change, NEWater and desalinated water are key weather-resilient sources that especially strengthen our water resilience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our water distribution network also remains one of the most efficient in the world, with water losses at about 8%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: PUB achieves this with regular maintenance and technology, such as sensors to detect and respond to pipe leaks early.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As we invest in building and maintaining our water infrastructure, we should also persist with our water conservation efforts to moderate the growth in water demand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will continue to work closely with stakeholders, from households to businesses, to shape behaviours and promote sustainable water use.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To address rising temperatures, we have developed a science-based, multi-pronged heat resilience strategy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As mentioned by Ms Valerie Lee, this is a whole-of-nation effort – academia, Government agencies and the community must come together so that Singapore continues to be a vibrant, liveable and dynamic city.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Ng Shi Xuan asked how we will harmonise standards and share best practices across existing heat resilience efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Tackling heat has been an ongoing work of the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For example, MSE has been enhancing public awareness on heat stress prevention through the Heat Stress Advisory and communication campaigns and the Ministry of National Development has been incorporating cooling strategies into our city's urban planning and building design, such as wind corridors to optimise wind flow and trees to provide shade along key pedestrian routes and public spaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We had also prepared the national heatwave response plan involving over 30 Government agencies and Ministries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The new Heat Resilience Policy Office will bring together efforts across various agencies, including the Ministry of National Development, the Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Manpower and the Ministry of Social and Family Development, to chart the way forward for our heat resilience efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will do so in three main ways: coordinate action, oversee research and represent us internationally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Office will develop a Heat Resilience Action Plan across the infrastructure, health, economic and social sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Action Plan will identify priority areas and develop measures to address them, including by extending proven solutions to other sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
